profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting about a sudden slowdown in a nightly model-transformation pipeline for a telecom configuration product line. The team uses an ATL/EMFTVM-based transformation to convert large architecture models into deployment descriptors and validation artifacts. Over the last week, the nightly job for one customer line jumped from roughly 11 minutes to 38 minutes, and leadership wants to know whether the issue comes from specific transformation rules, the runtime environment, or the surrounding pipeline. The agenda is to compare observations from transformation profiling and CI telemetry, agree on the likely root cause, and decide what diagnostic run and short-term mitigation should happen before tonight's build. The expected outcome is an agreed troubleshooting plan and a shared statement of what would count as having 'validated' a fix.

members.name: Lina Haddad
members.expertise: ATL/EMFTVM transformations, EMF model analysis, rule-level profiling, performance tuning of model-driven toolchains
members.background: Lina has spent six years building and maintaining model transformations for large industrial systems, especially transformations that generate deployment and configuration artifacts from architecture models.
members.private_state: Lina wants evidence that points to a specific transformation rule before anyone blames the transformation design broadly; she is also trying to avoid a rushed refactor that would destabilize the release branch.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'transformation time,' they mean the time spent executing ATL rules after the source model has already been loaded into EMF.
The 'baseline package' for performance discussions is the large representative benchmark model warehouse_v2_180k.xmi from the team's profiling suite, not the small CI fixture.
A fix is only really validated if it improves behavior on a cold run of the affected large model and removes the rule-level hotspot pattern.
The runtime environment used for recent nightly regressions is effectively the same across runners unless someone explicitly announced a rollout difference.

members.name: Ben Ko
members.role: Developer Productivity and Build Systems Engineer
members.expertise: CI/CD pipelines, JVM performance instrumentation, test runners, build observability, regression triage
members.background: Ben manages the infrastructure that runs nightly model-generation jobs, maintains timing dashboards for pipeline stages, and adds instrumentation when engineering teams report build regressions.
members.private_state: Ben wants a reproducible CI-level explanation he can act on quickly, ideally without introducing specialized instrumentation that only works on one engineer's workstation; he is also trying to keep tonight's pipeline green with minimal operational changes.
hidden_assumptions: When teams talk about the 'transformation' being slow, they usually mean the entire CI transform stage including XMI load, execution, serialization, and post-generation validation.
The 'baseline package' is the repository fixture baseline-orderflow.xmi because that is what nightly dashboards and smoke tests call baseline.
A fix is validated when repeated CI runs on the standard runner pool bring the transform stage back under the normal wall-clock threshold, regardless of which internal rule consumed the time.
Everyone involved in regression triage knows that last week's EMFTVM 5.7.2 rollout only reached the canary runner and not the full nightly fleet.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about 'transformation time' and 'profiling the transformation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the execution time of ATL rules inside EMFTVM, excluding model loading, serialization, and downstream validation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the whole CI transform stage wall-clock time, including XMI parsing, ATL execution, file writes, and the schema-validation step.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In both model-engineering and CI contexts, calling the whole activity 'the transformation' sounds completely natural, so the same phrase creates false consensus without either person feeling a need to separate internal rule time from stage time.

misalignment_points.topic: Which artifact is the baseline package
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'rerun the baseline package' before deciding on the root cause.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of warehouse_v2_180k.xmi, a large benchmark model from the performance suite that resembles the affected customer workload.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of baseline-orderflow.xmi, the smaller repository fixture used by nightly smoke tests and CI timing dashboards.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are routinely labeled 'baseline' in adjacent documentation and internal chat, and each participant mostly works in a context where only one of those baselines is commonly discussed.

misalignment_points.topic: What would count as validating the fix
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they want to 'validate the fix' and be 'good for tonight.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks validation means one cold run on the large affected model shows the hotspot rule no longer dominates and the slowdown does not reappear under realistic conditions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks validation means three repeated CI runs on the runner pool average under the usual wall-clock threshold for the transform stage, even if the internal hotspot pattern is still unclear.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using familiar operational language that usually goes unquestioned in urgent troubleshooting, and each assumes their team's normal acceptance ritual is the obvious one.

misalignment_points.topic: How far last week's runtime update spread
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'after the runtime update' as if they share the same deployment context.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the recent EMFTVM 5.7.2 runtime update had already landed on the nightly environment generally, so comparisons across recent runs are apples-to-apples.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes it is already understood that only the canary runner moved to 5.7.2 while most nightly jobs still execute on 5.6.9.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The rollout was mentioned in infra channels but not in the transformation team's working notes, so both can comfortably reference 'the update' while silently relying on different deployment scopes.

If there's a real regression, I want it tied to a rule hotspot, not used as justification for a broad refactor on the release branch.
